entities.summary:
Euthymus, a celebrated boxer from Epizephyrian Locris (modern-day southern Italy), emerged as a dominant athletic figure in the early 5th century BCE, a period when Greek city-states vied for supremacy and athletic contests served as crucial expressions of civic pride and individual excellence. Born around 600 BCE, Euthymus transcended mere athletic achievement, becoming a legendary hero whose life intertwined with local mythology and religious veneration, particularly in the cities of Locri and Temesa. His multiple victories at the ancient Olympic Games cemented his status as a paragon of physical prowess and moral fortitude, symbolizing the ideals of Hellenic masculinity and competitive spirit during the Classical era.

Euthymus achieved his first Olympic boxing victory at the 74th Olympiad in 484 BCE. Although he suffered a notable defeat to Theagenes of Thasos at the 75th Olympiad in 480 BCE, he avenged this loss by defeating Theagenes in a subsequent encounter, securing further Olympic titles in 476 BCE (76th Olympiad) and 472 BCE (77th Olympiad). His athletic career was immortalized through a statue crafted by Pythocritus of Rhegium, which Pausanias later observed at Olympia. Beyond the athletic arena, Euthymus is famously associated with the mythical expulsion of Lycas, a malevolent spirit or hero who terrorized the city of Temesa by demanding human sacrifices, a feat that cemented his heroic status and led to his posthumous cult.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Euthymus was a significant regional figure whose multiple Olympic victories and legendary heroic deeds established a lasting hero cult, providing valuable insight into the intersection of sport, myth, and religion in Classical Greece. His story, preserved by Pausanias, illustrates how exceptional human achievement could lead to posthumous veneration and civic identity.
